record.paper_title: Understanding Solar Flares and Energetic Events: Open questions, observational requirements, and instrumental needs over the coming decade
record.original_question: What is the magnitude, origin, and transport mechanism of the additional energy that must be deposited during the gradual phase of a solar flare, after the impulsive phase dominated by high-energy electrons, in order to explain cooling and mass-flow timescales that observed flares show but standard flare models fail to reproduce?

evidence.quote: 4. What is the magnitude, source, and transport mechanisms of energy deposition during the gradual phase? The ﬂare ‘impulsive phase’ has historically been viewed as the main energy release phase of ﬂares, typically deﬁned by the presence of high-energy electrons.

Though suppression of thermal conduction [48, 49] and accounting for non-equilibrium and non-Maxwellian plasmas [50] can perhaps mitigate this discrepancy, it is now widely recognised that additional energy must be deposited on longer timescales than implied by hard X-ray signatures from non-thermal electrons. Indeed, this might even require energy rivaling that of the impulsive phase [48]. The source and transport mechanism of this missing energy is almost completely unknown.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A solar flare is commonly modeled as a two-phase event. In the impulsive phase, magnetic reconnection in the corona accelerates a population of non-thermal electrons whose energy deposition into the chromosphere is inferred from hard X-ray bremsstrahlung emission; this energy then drives chromospheric evaporation and heats coronal loops to temperatures of order 10^7 K. In the subsequent gradual phase, the loops cool and drain on observed timescales (typically tens of minutes to hours), characterized by the temporal evolution of soft X-ray and EUV emission and by Doppler-measured mass flows.

Standard one-dimensional hydrodynamic flare loop models (e.g., field-aligned models with classical Spitzer thermal conduction, optically thin radiative losses, and a heating function calibrated to the hard X-ray–inferred non-thermal electron beam) predict cooling and draining timescales that are systematically shorter than those observed, even after allowing for suppression of thermal conduction and for non-equilibrium, non-Maxwellian plasma effects. To reconcile model and observation, an additional volumetric heating term Q_grad(s,t) (energy per unit volume per unit time, as a function of position s along the loop and time t) must be supplied during the gradual phase.

Determine:
(a) the total energy E_grad = ∫∫ Q_grad(s,t) A(s) ds dt deposited in a representative flare loop during the gradual phase, and in particular whether E_grad is comparable to the impulsive-phase energy deposited by non-thermal electrons;
(b) the physical origin of this additional energy (for example, continued or secondary magnetic reconnection, stored magnetohydrodynamic wave energy, turbulence, or a separate non-thermal particle population);
(c) the transport mechanism by which this energy is delivered to the radiating and flowing plasma (for example, Alfvén-wave Poynting flux, ion beams, suprathermal electrons not detected in hard X-rays, or in-situ heating by turbulent dissipation),
in such a way that a self-consistent loop model reproduces the observed gradual-phase cooling curves and mass-flow timescales.
artifact.status_search_result: The magnitude, source, and transport mechanism of the additional gradual-phase heating in solar flares is widely recognized as an unresolved problem in solar physics. Reviews and recent modeling work (Reep et al., Warren et al., Bradshaw & Cargill) acknowledge that standard electron-beam-driven models underpredict observed cooling/draining timescales and that the missing energy may rival that of the impulsive phase, with its source largely unknown.

status_evidence.title: Heating Rates in Solar Flares (Reep et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: Models of flare loops require additional heating beyond what electron beams deliver to match observed cooling timescales.
status_evidence.claim: Mainstream solar-flare modeling literature recognizes a missing gradual-phase heating component.

status_evidence.title: Bradshaw & Cargill, on coronal cooling discrepancies
status_evidence.snippet: Suppression of thermal conduction and non-equilibrium ionization can partially but not fully reconcile model cooling with observations.
status_evidence.claim: The discrepancy between modeled and observed flare cooling persists, motivating extended heating.
